content: Thiourea is an organic compound composed of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur, and hydrogen, with the chemical formula CSN₂H₄ or (NH₂)₂CS. Structurally, it is similar to urea, but the oxygen atom in urea is replaced by a sulfur atom in thiourea. This substitution leads to significant differences in their chemical properties due to the differing electronegativities of sulfur and oxygen. Thiourea is widely used as a versatile reagent in organic synthesis. The term thioureas refers to a broad class of compounds with the general structure (R₁R₂N)(R₃R₄N)C=S, where R groups can be alkyl groups such as methyl or ethyl. Thiourea is a planar molecule, and its C=S bond length is approximately 1 Å across a wide range of derivatives. This consistent bond length suggests that the C=S bond is relatively insensitive to the nature of substituents. The thioamide group, which is structurally similar to an amide group, is notably resistant to perturbation. Thiourea exists in two tautomeric forms. The global annual production of thiourea is approximately 10,000 tons, with around 40% produced in Germany, another 40% in China, and 20% in Japan. Thiourea can be synthesized from ammonium thiocyanate, but it is more commonly prepared by reacting hydrogen sulfide with calcium cyanamide in the presence of carbon dioxide. Many derivatives of thiourea are also valuable. N,N-unsubstituted thioureas are typically synthesized by reacting the corresponding cyanamide with lithium aluminum hydride sulfide (LiAlHSH) in the presence of 1N HCl in anhydrous diethyl ether. LiAlHSH itself is prepared by reacting sulfur with lithium aluminum hydride. Thiourea has several important applications. It reduces peroxides to their corresponding diols. The reaction proceeds through an unstable intermediate called an epidioxide, which can only be identified at extremely low temperatures (-100°C). Epidioxides are structurally similar to epoxides but contain two oxygen atoms. Thiourea facilitates the reduction of this intermediate to diols. Additionally, thiourea is used in the reductive workup of ozonolysis reactions to yield carbonyl compounds. Unlike urea, which is volatile and has an unpleasant odor, thiourea is odorless and non-volatile, reflecting its polar nature. Thiourea is commonly employed to convert alkyl halides into thiols. This reaction leverages the high nucleophilicity of the sulfur atom in thiourea and the hydrolytic instability of the resulting isothiuronium salt. While alkali metal sulfides could also be used for this conversion, thiourea avoids the formation of dialkyl sulfides, which are undesirable side products often encountered with reagents like Na₂S. Thioureas are also used as building blocks for synthesizing pyrimidine derivatives. In these reactions, thioureas condense with β-dicarbonyl compounds. The amino group on thiourea initially reacts with a carbonyl group, followed by cyclization and tautomerization, ultimately yielding pyrimidines. Similarly, aminothiazoles can be synthesized by reacting alpha-halo ketones with thiourea. Another significant application of thiourea is as a sulfur source for the synthesis of semiconductor cadmium sulfide (CdS) nanoparticles. In this process, a colorless slurry solution changes to yellow, indicating the formation of CdS. Industrially, thiourea is also used in the production of flame-retardant resins and as a vulcanization accelerator. It serves as an auxiliary agent in the production of diazo paper (light-sensitive photocopy paper) and other types of copy paper. The liquid silver-cleaning product Tarn-X is essentially a solution of thiourea. Additionally, thiourea can be selectively oxidized to create a leaching agent for gold and silver extraction, bypassing the need for cyanide and smelting processes. Regarding safety, thiourea has been reported to have goitrogenic effects, leading to the enlargement of the thyroid gland. Chronic administration in rats has been associated with the development of hepatic tumors. Bone marrow depression has also been reported as a potential adverse effect.
